In [[functional analysis]], '''Namioka's theorem''' is a result concerning the relationship between [[separate and joint continuity|separate continuity and joint continuity]] of functions defined on [[Inner product space|product spaces]]. Named after [[mathematician]] [[Isaac Namioka]], who proved it in his 1974 paper ''Separate Continuity and Joint Continuity'' published in the [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]], the theorem establishes conditions under which a separately continuous function must be jointly continuous on a topologically large subset of its [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]].<ref name="Namioka-1974">Namioka, I. (1974). "Separate continuity and joint continuity". [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]], 51(2), 515-531.</ref>

== Statement ==
<blockquote>'''Namioka's theorem'''. Let <math>X</math> be a [[Čech-complete]] [[topological space]] (such as a [[complete metric space]]), <math>Y</math> be a [[compact space|compact]] [[Hausdorff space]], and <math>Z</math> be a [[metric space]]. If <math>f: X \times Y \rightarrow Z</math> is ''separately continuous'', meaning that
* for each fixed <math>x_0 \in X</math>, the function <math>y \mapsto f(x_0, y)</math> is continuous on <math>Y</math>, and
* for each fixed <math>y_0 \in Y</math>, the function <math>x \mapsto f(x, y_0)</math> is continuous on <math>X</math>,
then there exists a [[dense set|dense]] [[Gδ set|<math>G_\delta</math>-subset]] <math>G</math> of <math>X</math> such that <math>f</math> is jointly continuous at each point of <math>G \times Y</math>.<ref name="Namioka-1974"/><ref name="Stegall-1988">Stegall, C. (1988). "Generalizations of a theorem of Namioka". Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society, 102(3), 559-564.</ref></blockquote>

Namioka's theorem can be equivalently stated in terms of the set <math>C(f)</math> of points where <math>f</math> is continuous, stating that the [[projection (mathematics)|projection]] of <math>C(f)</math> onto <math>X</math> contains a dense <math>G_\delta</math> subset of <math>X</math>.<ref name="Namioka-1974"/><ref name="Stegall-1988"/>

== History ==
French mathematician [[René Baire]] was among the first to systematically study the relationship between separate and joint continuity in 1899, for [[real-valued functions]] of real variables.<ref>Baire, R. (1899). "Sur les fonctions des variables réelles". Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata, 3, 1-122.</ref> Austrian mathematician [[Hans Hahn (mathematician)|Hans Hahn]] later extended these investigations in 1932, proving similar results for functions defined on complete metric spaces.<ref>Hahn, H. (1932). Reelle Funktionen. Leipzig, pp. 325-338.</ref> Namioka generalized these results to [[Metrizable space|non-metrizable spaces]], particularly to Čech-complete spaces, which include all complete metric spaces as a [[special case]]. There exists a proof using tools from [[general topology]] such as the Arkhangel'skii–Frolík covering theorem and the [[Kuratowski and Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem]].<ref name="Stegall-1988"/>
